# A thermodynamically consistent body: Langevin noise {#sec-langevin}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
**Status:** draft · **Updated:** 2026-11-21 · **Checked by:** `tests/test_energy_whitening.py`
:::

The noise of Part I is static: a fresh draw from $\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2\Em^{-1})$ laid over
the state at each sample, independent from one sample to the next. A body that is
physically noisy is driven instead by thermal forces matched to its own dampers, and its
noise is shaped by its dynamics. This chapter builds that model and asks whether the
conclusions of Part I survive.

**The model.** The equation of motion becomes
$$
  H\ddot q+D\dot q+Kq=J^\top f(t)+\xi(t),\qquad
  \E[\xi(t)\xi(s)^\top]=2\sigma_T^2D\,\delta(t-s),
$$
started from the Gibbs law $x_q(0)\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_T^2\Em^{-1})$ on the clamped
bench. By @prp-fdt the noise is stationary at covariance $P=\sigma_T^2\Em^{-1}$.
Sampling with step $\Delta t$ gives $x_{k+1}=A_dx_k+B_df_k+w_k$ with $w_k$ i.i.d.
$\mathcal N(0,Q_d)$ and $Q_d=P-A_dPA_d^\top$; this is `gibbs_pair`, scaled by
$\sigma_T^2$. We set $\sigma_T^2=\sigma^2=10^{-4}$ J, so a snapshot of the noise has
exactly the covariance used in Part I. Only its correlation over time differs.

::: {#prp-innov name="Full observation: an exact formula"}
If the whole state is observed and the only noise is thermal, the information about the
force profile is
$$
  \bits=\tfrac12\log_2\det\!\big(I_d+\sigma_w^2\,g\,\bar\Phi^\top\bar\Phi\big),
  \qquad g=B_d^\top Q_d^{-1}B_d ,
$$
where $\bar\Phi$ holds the force basis at the samples that drive the state. The design
enters only through the scalar $g$, the per-sample signal-to-noise ratio of a unit force
against one thermal kick.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Step 1: change variables.* The map from $(x_0,x_1,\dots,x_N)$ to
$(x_0,e_0,\dots,e_{N-1})$, with $e_k=x_{k+1}-A_dx_k$, is invertible. So the two carry the
same information (@lem-noise(a)).

*Step 2: what the new variables contain.* $x_0$ is independent of the force, and
$e_k=B_df_k+w_k$, where the $w_k$ are i.i.d., independent of $x_0$, and Gaussian with
covariance $Q_d$. This is a Gaussian channel with noise covariance $I\otimes Q_d$.

*Step 3: apply the Gaussian formula.* Whiten the noise by $Q_d^{-1/2}$ and apply
@lem-gauss with $f_k=\sum_jw_j\bar\Phi_{kj}$. The Gram matrix is
$\sigma_w^2\sum_k\bar\Phi_k^\top(B_d^\top Q_d^{-1}B_d)\bar\Phi_k$, where $\bar\Phi_k$ is
row $k$ of $\bar\Phi$. Since $g$ is a scalar, this equals $\sigma_w^2g\,\bar\Phi^\top\bar\Phi$.
:::

::: {#prp-contact name="Only the dissipation at the contact matters"}
Suppose $J^\top$ lies in the range of $D$. As $\Delta t\to0$,
$$
  g\;\to\;\frac{\Delta t}{2\sigma_T^2}\,J D^+J^\top .
$$
With the full state observed, the information therefore depends only on $JD^+J^\top$: the
damping seen at the point where the force acts. For the ground model used here, $JD^+J^\top=1/b_i$
for the rigid transmission and for every SEA, so every design gives the same bits.
:::

::: {.proof name="Proof sketch"}
*Continuous time.* In the continuous-time limit, observing the state exactly is a
white-Gaussian-noise channel for the drift $Bf$, with noise intensity
$GG^\top=\diag(0,\,2\sigma_T^2H^{-1}DH^{-1})$. In the low-signal limit, where the causal
estimate of the signal is negligible, Duncan's theorem [@duncan1970calculation] gives
the information rate $\frac12\E[(Bf)^\top(GG^\top)^+(Bf)]$ nats per second.

*The rate.* Substituting $B=[0;H^{-1}J^\top]$ gives
$$
  \tfrac12\E[f^2]\,JH^{-1}\big(2\sigma_T^2H^{-1}DH^{-1}\big)^+H^{-1}J^\top
  =\frac{\E[f^2]}{4\sigma_T^2}\,JD^+J^\top .
$$

*Matching to the discrete channel.* Over one sample, the discrete channel carries
$\frac12\log(1+g\,\E[f^2])\approx\frac12g\,\E[f^2]$ nats about a force sample. The
continuous rate gives $\Delta t\,\E[f^2]\,JD^+J^\top/(4\sigma_T^2)$ over the same
interval. Equating the two gives the stated limit for $g$, which does not depend on the
signal amplitude.

*The design-independence.*

- For the rigid leg, $D=b_ir^2$ and $J=-r$, so $JD^+J^\top=1/b_i$.
- For the SEA,
    $D=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}b_s+b_ir^2&-b_s\\-b_s&b_s\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ has
    $\det D=b_sb_ir^2$, so $(D^{-1})_{11}=b_s/(b_sb_ir^2)=1/(b_ir^2)$. With
    $J=(-r,0)$, this gives $JD^{-1}J^\top=1/b_i$, independently of $k_s$ and $b_s$.

*What is not proved here.* We do not prove that the discrete position-block terms
leave the constant unchanged. The numbers below confirm it.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Numerical check"}

- $2\sigma_T^2 g/(\Delta t\,JD^+J^\top)$ is $1.0000$ at 4, 16 and 64 kHz for the
    rigid leg and for SEAs at $k_s=70$, $10^4$ and $10^6$ (shown as $g\sigma_T^2
        f_s/JD^+J^\top=0.5000$ by `check_langevin_dt_limit`). It deviates only for
    coarse sampling (0.19 at 100 Hz).
- The exact formula of @prp-innov and a direct computation with the full
    stacked noise covariance agree, 37.74216 bits
    (`check_langevin_innovations`).
- At the settings of @sec-setup, *every* design gives 37.742 bits with the full state
    observed.

:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="What this means physically"}
This is the thermal limit on what a body can hold about a force. The force competes
with the fluctuating force of the damper at the contact, whose strength is set by the
fluctuation-dissipation theorem (the mechanical analogue of Johnson-Nyquist noise [@nyquist1928thermal]). If the whole state is observed, the body's inertia and
stiffness are irrelevant: no morphology can beat the contact-damper limit.

The body's design matters when we ask what a *part* of the body holds, such as the rotor
or the link. Each internal damper between the contact and that part adds thermal noise
on the way.
:::

**What a part holds: where morphology enters.** A part of the body is a set of its
coordinates, picked out of $x_q$ by a selector $C$ (the rotor's angle, say). With noise
injected through the dampers, the part's trajectory gives the Gram matrix
$\sigma_w^2M_C^\top(C\Sigma C^\top)^{-1}M_C$. Here $\Sigma$ is the stacked noise
covariance, with blocks $\Cov(x_k,x_l)=A_d^{k-l}P$ for $k\ge l$ (`langevin_bits`; a
diagonal of $10^{-9}$ is added for numerical conditioning only). A part is a function of
the whole state, so by data processing no part can hold more than the whole body. The
37.742 bits are a hard ceiling for every part of every design.

| Design | Langevin: whole body | Langevin: rotor | Share | Static: whole body | Static: rotor | Share |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| rigid | 37.742 | 37.695 | 0.999 | 71.723 | 66.836 | 0.932 |
| SEA, $k_s=70$ | 37.742 | 2.266 | 0.060 | 69.280 | 2.566 | 0.037 |
| SEA, $10^3$ | 37.742 | 18.628 | 0.494 | 70.267 | 38.252 | 0.544 |
| SEA, $3\times10^3$ | 37.742 | 29.038 | 0.769 | 71.084 | 55.097 | 0.775 |
| SEA, $10^4$ | 37.742 | 35.067 | 0.929 | 71.773 | 60.988 | 0.850 |
| SEA, $10^5$ | 37.742 | 37.242 | 0.987 | 71.742 | 65.943 | 0.919 |

: Bits about the force profile ($B_w=100$ Hz) held by the whole body and by the rotor's angle, under the Langevin body and under the static noise of Part I (`check_langevin_designs`). Share is rotor bits divided by whole-body bits. Under static noise the rotor's angle carries variance $\sigma^2(\Em^{-1})_{rr}$. {#tbl-langevin}

Three findings (@tbl-langevin; @fig-langevin):

1. *Through a rigid transmission the force reaches the rotor almost intact.*
    The rigid rotor's angle holds 99.9% of the thermal ceiling. The SEA rotor's share
    rises monotonically with stiffness: 6% at the prototype's $k_s=70$, 49% at $10^3$,
    93% at $10^4$, 99.5% at $10^6$. The series damper sits between the contact and the
    rotor, and its thermal force erodes what arrives. With no damper on the way, as in
    the rigid leg, nothing is lost. The research note on
    [information propagation](../notes/2026-11-21-information-propagation.qmd) turns this
    into a formula: a part holds the force as if the contact damping were larger, by an
    amount set by the internal dampers between the contact and the part. The same
    reasoning underlies the case of @wensing2017proprioceptive for proprioceptive
    actuation, here derived from the mechanics alone.
2. *Energy noise ranks the rotors the same way, static or thermal.* Under static energy
    noise no SEA rotor beats the rigid rotor either, and the SEA's share climbs with
    stiffness through nearly the same values up to $3\times10^3$. A soft series spring
    amplifies the force at the rotor, and under energy noise it amplifies the noise there
    by the same factor, through $(\Em^{-1})_{rr}$ in the static case and through
    fluctuation-dissipation in the thermal one. A fixed angle noise of $10^{-4}$ rad,
    the per-coordinate metric of @sec-alternatives, misses this: it lets the SEA rotor
    at $k_s=3\times10^3$ beat the rigid rotor by 5.9 bits, because it counts the
    amplified signal and ignores the amplified noise.
3. *The two noise models differ in level and in what a coordinate's velocity adds.*
    Static noise gives 69.3 to 71.8 bits for the whole body against 37.742 under
    Langevin noise, because fresh independent noise at each sample averages down while
    thermal noise is correlated over time. Static noise also leaves the rigid rotor's
    angle 7% short of the whole body, where Langevin noise leaves it 0.1% short. Under
    static noise the velocity carries noise independent of the angle's, so it adds a
    second look at the force. Under thermal noise the velocity is the derivative of the
    angle, noise included, so the angle's trajectory already holds what the velocity
    holds.

**Caveats.**

- $\sigma_T^2$ is an effective temperature, chosen to match Part I.
- The ground damping $b_i$ is a modeling choice ($\zeta_{\rm contact}=0.15$),
    identical across designs by construction (the analysis library checks this in
    `test_one_ground_for_every_design`). The common ceiling is therefore a
    property of the ground model.
- Damping is modeled as constant and viscous. The model needs a positive-definite
    $\Em$, so it applies to the clamped bench only.
